title: Pinot Noir
description: Also called Spätburgunder in Germany and Pinot Nero in Italy. Thin skin, high acid and a talent for showing where it was grown.
L: Why the palest red is the hardest to grow
Explain why Pinot Noir is pale

Pinot Noir gives pale to medium ruby wines with red cherry, raspberry, strawberry and, with age, earthy notes of mushroom, forest floor and game. Tannins are low to medium and silky, acidity high. Its delicacy and complexity make it one of the most prized grapes, and Burgundy is its home.

Pinot Noir's skins are thin and low in colour pigments, so its wines are pale and low in tannin. Its tight bunches, shaped like a pine cone, which may give it its name, trap moisture and invite rot. It buds early, risking frost, and mutates easily, with hundreds of clones. It's one of the oldest known grapes, recorded in Burgundy in the 14th century.
Why is Pinot Noir usually pale in colour?
Its skins are thin and low in pigment
Thin skins with few pigments give pale colour and low tannin.

Look for pale ruby, translucent colour. On the nose, red cherry, raspberry and often earthy or floral notes. On the palate, high acidity, silky low tannin and a long, fine finish. If you can read a page through the wine and it smells of red fruit and earth, think Pinot Noir.
Pinot Noir's tight bunches make it prone to rot.
Yes. Tight, compact bunches trap moisture, inviting rot in damp weather.
Pinot Noir is pale because of thin, low-pigment skins
It smells of red fruit and, with age, earth and mushroom
Explain why it needs a cool climate

Pinot Noir needs a cool climate. In heat, it ripens too fast, losing its delicate aromas and acidity and turning jammy. A long, cool season builds complexity. Its main homes are Burgundy, Champagne, Germany, Oregon, California's coast, New Zealand, Chile's coast, Australia's Victoria and Tasmania.

Pinot Noir mutates easily, so there are hundreds of clones, each with different berry size, yield and flavour. Dijon clones, like 115, 667 and 777, developed in Burgundy, spread worldwide from the 1980s. California's Pommard and Wädenswil clones are also widely planted. Many growers plant several clones for complexity.
What happens to Pinot Noir in a hot climate?
It ripens too fast, losing aroma and turning jammy
Heat speeds ripening, losing the delicacy Pinot is prized for.

Pinot Noir is the parent or ancestor of many grapes. Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc are colour mutations; Meunier is another mutation. Crossed with Gouais Blanc, it gave Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté and Melon. That makes it one of the most important grapes in the history of wine.
Which grapes are mutations of Pinot Noir?
Pinot Noir needs a cool climate
Hundreds of clones, like the Dijon clones, exist
It's the ancestor of Chardonnay, Gamay and others

The Côte d'Or, the golden slope, is a narrow strip of east and south-east facing vineyards about 50 km long, from Dijon to Santenay. The north, the Côte de Nuits, is mostly Pinot Noir. The south, the Côte de Beaune, makes both reds and Chardonnay. Limestone and marl soils, and mid-slope positions, give the best wines.
Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune

Burgundy ranks vineyards: Grand Cru at the top, then Premier Cru, then village wines, then regional Bourgogne. Grand Crus like Romanée-Conti, Chambertin and Musigny name only the vineyard on the label. Of Burgundy's 33 Grand Crus, most of the reds are in the Côte de Nuits. Each climat has its own character.
Grand Cru, Premier Cru, village, regional
Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
Each level narrows the area and raises expectations.

Gevrey-Chambertin gives powerful, structured reds; Chambolle-Musigny elegant, perfumed ones; Vosne-Romanée rich, spicy and silky, home to Romanée-Conti. In the Côte de Beaune, Pommard is firm, Volnay delicate. Same grape, different soils and slopes, distinct wines.
Match each village to its style.
Each Burgundy village has its own personality.
The Côte d'Or runs from Dijon to Santenay
Burgundy ranks climats from regional to Grand Cru
Each village, like Gevrey or Chambolle, has its own style
Explain Pinot Noir's role in Champagne

Pinot Noir is about 38% of Champagne's vineyards, the most planted grape there. It gives body, structure and red fruit aromas to blends. The Montagne de Reims, with Grand Crus like Aÿ, Bouzy and Verzenay, and the Côte des Bar, in the south, are its strongholds.

Since the colour is in the skins, gentle pressing of whole bunches gives a pale, white juice from black grapes. Blanc de Noirs is white Champagne made only from Pinot Noir and/or Meunier. It's fuller and fruitier than Blanc de Blancs. For rosé Champagne, a little still red Pinot Noir is often blended in.
Blanc de Noirs: white from black
How can Champagne make white wine from Pinot Noir?
By gentle pressing that keeps the colour out
Colour is in the skins; gentle whole-bunch pressing keeps it out of the juice.

Bouzy, in the Montagne de Reims, is famous for still red wine, sold as Coteaux Champenois rouge. In warmer years, more producers make it. Its light, crisp style shows Pinot Noir at the edge of ripeness, a reminder of how cool Champagne is.
Pinot Noir is the most planted grape in Champagne.
Pinot Noir is Champagne's most planted grape, giving body
Blanc de Noirs is white Champagne from black grapes
Bouzy makes still red Coteaux Champenois

Germany is the world's third largest Pinot Noir producer, after France and the US, as Spätburgunder. Warmer vintages and better winemaking have transformed it since the 1990s. Baden, the Pfalz and the Ahr make elegant, increasingly respected wines, some rivalling good Burgundy.

Oregon's Willamette Valley, at Burgundy's latitude, makes Pinot Noir with bright fruit and earthy notes. In California, the Sonoma Coast, Russian River Valley, Santa Rita Hills and Anderson Valley, cooled by ocean fog and wind, give riper, fuller styles. The 2004 film Sideways boosted US Pinot sales.
Match each region to its Pinot Noir.
Cool climates around the world grow fine Pinot.

Pinot Noir is New Zealand's most planted red. Central Otago, the southernmost major wine region, gives vivid, fruity wines with fresh acidity. Martinborough gives savoury, structured wines; Marlborough lighter, fruit-driven ones. Australia's Yarra Valley, Mornington and Tasmania also excel.
What is Pinot Noir called in Germany?
Germany's Spätburgunder is now respected worldwide
Oregon and coastal California make fine Pinot
New Zealand's Central Otago leads the southern hemisphere

Pinot Noir's low tannin and high acidity make it one of the most food-friendly reds. It suits roast chicken, duck, salmon, tuna, mushrooms and game birds. Burgundy matches boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin. Its low tannin even works with some fish.

Serve at 14 to 16 degrees, slightly cooler than big reds, in a large bowl glass. Simple Pinot is best within five years. Top Burgundy ages 10 to 30 years, developing mushroom, truffle, game and forest floor. Decanting isn't always needed; it can lose delicate aromas.
Why does Pinot Noir pair well with salmon?
Its low tannin doesn't clash with fish
High tannin can make fish taste metallic; Pinot's low tannin avoids that.
Mushroom risotto with an older Pinot Noir is a near-perfect match. The earthy notes in both bring each other forward.
Very hot curry clashes with most reds.
Pinot Noir suits duck, salmon and mushrooms
Serve at 14 to 16 degrees in a large glass
Why is Pinot Noir hard to grow?
Thin skins, tight bunches and early budding
Its thin skins and tight bunches invite rot, and early budding risks frost.
